replies.author: SuperbActuator6555
replies.body:
Haha yeah, I know jack shit about game dev so you're probably totally right from a pure software perspective.

My issue is purely psychological/motivational. If I spend weeks coding backend logic and systems in a blank gray box, I’ll lose all my drive. For me, seeing a world that actually looks aliveeven just a small test scene with decent trees, lighting, and foliage is what makes me want to keep logging in and working on it.

Plus, basic movement, attacks, and quests are already pretty solved problems in terms of tutorials and assets, but getting a custom art style to look good in-engine was the big question mark in my head. Now that I know I *can* actually make a nice-looking environment, I feel way more motivated to start building the actual gameplay mechanics on top of it.

comments.author: Professional_Ask3718
comments.body:
Its a passion project, so if doing art first helps you, go nuts. Just dont overlook early design documentation. AI works really well when it has a blueprint of your vision. Start with themes and rules. How do you want your game to feel? From there, you can translate that into your art and other systems. "I want this game to feel warm and cosy" might translate into lots of soft reds and yellows and rounded edges for example. 

Having these themes and rules can also help it call you out when you start going off track. Scope creep can be a real issue for AI development because its so easy to add new features. For example you ask for an axe with gore dripping off of it, AI will often return "that clashes with our warm and cosy theme, are you sure you want to add that?"

It also keeps your assets from looking like they belong to completely different worlds
